According to the textbooks, this mixing of tribes and tongues, of Saxon settlers and British natives slowly gave rise to what we now call Englishness.

But this explanation, for all its perfection, doesn't tell the whole story. It doesn't explain the deeper symbols, the sacred bonds, the twin founders, the sword in the earth, the dragon curled around a horde, the fire in the sky and the king in the sun.

It doesn't explain why the earliest myths of England came not just from Saxony or Wales, but from somewhere older, from the endless grasslands beyond the Black Sea, from the windswept silence of the steppes, from Scythia, from Hyperborea.

The oldest songs of the English are like dreams remembered from another life, full of horse warriors, sun symbols, and rites that come not from the forests of Germania, nor the hills of Britain, but from the vast steps beyond the dawn.

The heroic code in Beowulf, blood loyalty, warrior kings, dragon slaying, and the centrality of the sword matches Sarmatian war ideology.

The twin founders, Hengist and Horsa, don't just appear out of thin air. They follow a pattern found across Indo-European myth, the divine twins.

This same ideology appears in Vedic India, the Asvins, in Greek mythology, Castor and Pollux, and in the founding of Rome itself with Romulus and Remus.

Twin brothers, one dies, one survives, one becomes king. In every case, the twins represent more than just brothers.

They symbolize duality, founding violence, divine ancestry, and the birth of a people.

Hengist and Horsa aren't just names in a chronicle. They're part of an Indo-European structure that predates England and even Rome.

The figure of the sacred sword in a Therian legend is consistent with Scythian religious practice, where the sword was not just a weapon, but a divine symbol often driven into the earth and worshipped.

More than half the world's population today derives between 5% and 40% of their genomes from a ghost group we only recognised after sequencing a 24,000 year old Siberian boy.

Since then, each new study has raised more questions than answers. In Libya's Takakori Caves, DNA extracted from 9,000 year old human remains revealed a lineage unrelated to any living African or Eurasian group.

High resolution sequencing showed these people carried genetic variants absent from every population on Earth today.

In the late 1920s, Soviet archaeologist Mikhail Gerasimov began excavating the Malta-Bure camps on Lake Baikal, excavating a semi-subterranean village built from mammoth bones and reindeer antler, roofed with animal skins to ward off the Siberian cold.

His teams recovered over 800 carved ivory and bone objects, Venus figures in detailed hoods, bird sculptures and mammoth tusk plates with geometric designs.

This is evidence of an ancient tradition and culture far beyond mere survival. Decades later, when researchers finally decoded the genome of the Malta child, they uncovered something astonishing that between 5 and 40% of modern Europeans and Native Americans trace their ancestry to this long lost population.

Coalescent models show that the Malta population's genetic lineage split from the ancestors of all other Homo sapiens around 40,000 to 50,000 years ago.

This doesn't mean the Malta people were isolated for millennia, but their DNA reveals a distinct branch of our species story.

We are not the outbreak of a single diaspora fading all else in its path. We are the product of many lineages, some of which vanished entirely.

If one genome from a Siberian child can change the scientific consensus that our ancestors came from at least one other human branch, then every other buried genome or hidden fossil suddenly becomes a potential revolver, pointed at our origin myths.

In the Tadrach Akakus of Libya, two women were buried between around 5200 BC and 4300 BC.

At first glance, their burials looked like any other early pastoralist site, but when Nader Salem's team sequenced their genomes, the results didn't fit.

These Takakori herders carried a North African ancestry component so distinct it remained unchanged through the green Sahara before disappearing once more.

One stranger, they show just 0.15%. Neanderthal DNA 10 times less than Levantine farmers and far above the 0% of most Sub-Saharan Africans.

What does this tell us? A community with only the slightest mix of outside genes.

Their closest genetic cousins come from the Epipelolithic foragers of Tafferalt Cave in Morocco, but even that link is faint, which shows how uniquely isolated the Takakori people were.

What forced these people into oblivion, the climate that turned grasslands to desert or newcomers who replaced them?

And if Africa hid this branch for millennia, what other lost peoples are buried under shifting dunes, alpine ice or arctic permafrost waiting to rewrite our origin story?

Takakori's story shows us that Africa wasn't one melting pot population, but a mosaic of peoples whose lives and legacies can disappear without warning.

That fragility is a real lesson. Every community we fail to remember is one fewer piece in our puzzle of identity and one more victory for the forces that prefer a simple, single-threaded past.

In September 1991, high in the Ötstahl Alps on the border of Austria and Italy, hikers stumbled upon the naturally mummified body of a man, later named Ötzi, preserved in ice for over 5,000 years.

Genetic analyses have since revealed that his Y chromosome haplogroup was G2A2B and his mitochondrial haplogroup was K1O, both rare or extinct in Europe today.

The really strange thing about this is the whole genome sequencing shows that Ötzi carried no step ancestry, none at all, the hallmark of later Bronze Age migrations and instead his autosomal profile clusters closest with early Neolithic farmers from Anatolia and the Aegean, yet still distinct enough to represent a lineage now vanished from the modern gene pool.

Even more bizarre, runs of homozygosity in Ötzi's genome meant his community was small and isolated, with an effective population size estimated at just a few hundred individuals.

That isolation, combined with his unique haplogroups, means that the alpine farmers of 3300 BCE worked and died in villages whose descendants were later replaced or mixed with other tribes, leaving Ötzi as one of the last of his kind.

What forced this alpine lineage into oblivion? Was it the influx of Yamnaya-derived steppe pastoralists during the Bronze Age?

Or did environmental shifts and epidemic waves gradually erode these early farming communities?

And for people who once lived on these slopes, could vanish so completely, what other mountain dwelling or valley dwelling populations have not been discovered and could give us a whole new branch of our history? That we are blank slates. That children are created purely by environment. That you can mold a person however you want if you just use the right words, the right schooling, the right ideology.

But what we now know is this. Inherited DNA differences account for between 30 and 60 percent of the variation in most psychological traits.

Take the Swedish adoption twin study of aging, Sätse for instance. In the early 1990s Plomin and his colleagues studied older twins, some reared apart, some together, to investigate the causes of stressful life events.

Using the social readjustment rating scale, which includes real-world events like illness, job loss and the death of a spouse, they found that identical twins were twice as similar as fraternal twins in how they responded to these events, even if raised in entirely different households.

This pointed to a heritability of roughly 30 percent for what had always been assumed to be purely environmental events.

In other words, how we perceive and respond to life stress is significantly shaped by our genes.

Another case, divorce. In a twin study of over 1,500 adult sibling pairs, concordance rates for divorce were 55 percent for identical twins and 16 percent for fraternal twins, suggesting an underlying genetic influence.

This definitely wasn't a fluke. A later adoption study in Sweden followed 20,000 adopted individuals and found that their likelihood of divorce was more strongly connected to whether their biological parents had divorced than whether their adoptive parents had.

This clearly wasn't environmental factors, but their DNA. And our ancestors already knew.

Diodorus Seculis's Bibliothica Historica. Diodorus Seculis was a Greek historian from Argoerion in Sicily, who lived during the first century BCE around 90 to 30 BCE.

He is best known for this massive work, the Bibliothica Historica, Library of History, a universal history spanning mythological origins to his own time.

This epically ambitious 40-book project aimed to chronicle the known world's history and culture, though sadly, only books 1-5 and 11-20 survive, with fragments of the rest preserved through later writers.

Diodorus Seculis's Bibliothica Historica provides some of the most vivid and detailed descriptions of the Celts from a classical perspective.

His account, largely based on earlier sources like Pussydanius, captures their appearance, customs, and way of life on their love of debate and eloquence.

At Daimbury and Sudden Farm in Hampshire, central southern Britain a study examined human remains found in two Iron Age sites.

In the past there was a lot of debate among archaeologists about how the Celtic people buried their dead.

Unlike today where we have formal ceremonies for burial, they didn't have many cemeteries back then.

Instead human remains were often found in unusual ways like just parts of a body or even a single bone, sometimes in storage pits.

This made it challenging to understand how they treated their dead. To understand this, researchers looked at the bones under microscopes using a special method called thin section light microscopy.

They used the Oxford histological index OHI to analyze the bones in detail. The results showed that different types of burial practices were used and the treatment of remains varied depending on the situation.

Some bones showed signs of being taken out of the ground and certain parts being removed before buried again.

Others seem to have been exposed to the elements before being buried. Only one sample showed evidence of a practice called ex-carnation which means leaving the dead body out in the open for a period before burial.

The research suggests that ancient people in Iron Age Britain had diverse ways of burying their dead.

They didn't just do the same thing for everybody. Instead they followed different rituals and treatments based on the specific circumstances.

This information helps us to understand how they practice their burial customs and gives us a glimpse into the beliefs and traditions about death and the afterlife.

The Urnfield Culture refers to a late Bronze Age civilisation that flourished across much of Europe, particularly in Central Europe, from around 1300 to 750 BC.

This culture is named after its distinctive funerary practice which involved cremating the dead and burying their ashes in urns that were then buried in fields.

The people of the Urnfield Culture were skilled metal workers, with bronze being the dominant material for making tools, weapons and ornaments.

Innovations in bronze metallurgy during this period included the widespread use of socketed axes and the introduction of new types of swords and spearheads.

Different advancements in bronze metallurgy marked a technological revolution that transformed daily life and warfare.

One of the key innovations was the development of socketed axes, which featured a hollow shaft allowing for a secure attachment of the handle, reducing the risk of detachment during use.

These axes, along with new types of swords and spearheads, were typically cast in two-piece moulds, enhancing their uniformity and strength.

The swords of this era were longer and designed for both slashing and stabbing, a significant evolution from the shorter stabbing swords of earlier periods.

The introduction of flanged edges and decorative hilts not only increased the functionality of these weapons, but also their aesthetic appeal, indicating the high craftsmanship of Urnfield metal workers.

These advancements had profound impacts on Urnfield society, influencing both warfare and social structure.

Improved weapons allowed for more effective combat and the conduct of warfare on a larger scale, while the skilled artisans capable of producing these complex items likely held a significant status within their communities.

This period also saw spearheads becoming larger and incorporating elaborate designs, suggesting a blend of practicality and ceremonial use.
